smt-2022-power-2-1a.prompt: A coin lands heads with probability $p$ on each flip, independently. Let $X\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p)$ be the number of flips until the first head. Justify that $P[X=x]=(1-p)^{x-1}p$ for $x\ge1$.

smt-2022-power-2-1b.prompt: A coin lands heads with probability $p$ on each flip, independently. Let $X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ be the number of heads in $n$ flips. Justify that $P[X=x]=\binom nxp^x(1-p)^{n-x}$ for $0\le x\le n$.

smt-2022-power-2-2.prompt: Recall that a random variable $X$ with probability density function $p_X$ has $\mathbb E[X]=\int xp_X(x)\,dx$ (for a variable on the nonnegative integers, $\sum_{n\ge0}n\,p_X(n)$), $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2$, $z$-transform $\widehat X(z)=\mathbb E[z^X]$ and moment generating function $\widetilde X(s)=\mathbb E[e^{sX}]$. Prove that the derivatives of the moment generating function are the moments of $X$: $\widetilde X^{(k)}(0)=\mathbb E[X^k]$ (the $k$-th derivative evaluated at $s=0$). You may differentiate under the integral (or sum) sign.

smt-2022-power-2-3a.prompt: If $X\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p)$ (the number of flips of a $p$-biased coin up to and including the first head), compute $\mathbb E[X]$ in terms of $p$. Show your work.

smt-2022-power-2-3b.prompt: If $X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ (the number of heads in $n$ independent flips of a $p$-biased coin), compute $\mathbb E[X]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and the $z$-transform $\widehat X(z)=\mathbb E[z^X]$ in terms of $n$ and $p$. Show your work. You may use that expectation is linear and that variances of independent variables add.

smt-2022-power-2-3c.prompt: If $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, so that $P[X=k]=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}$, compute $\mathbb E[X]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and the $z$-transform $\widehat X(z)=\mathbb E[z^X]$ in terms of $\lambda$. Show your work.

smt-2022-power-2-4.prompt: Let $X_n\sim\mathrm{Binomial}\left(n,\frac\lambda n\right)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, where $Y$ models the number of arrivals in one hour at a fixed rate $\lambda$, while $X_n$ can be viewed as flipping $n$ coins at times $\frac1n,\frac2n,\dots,1$, counting heads. Briefly give some intuition for how $X_n$ and $Y$ are connected as $n\to\infty$.
smt-2022-power-2-4.answer: As $n\to\infty$ the coin flips become infinitesimally close in time, each independent with total expected number of heads $\lambda$, which is exactly the model of fixed-rate, memoryless arrivals, i.e. a Poisson variable.

smt-2022-power-2-5.prompt: Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in the nonnegative integers with $z$-transform $\widehat X(z)=\mathbb E[z^X]$. Find an expression for $p_X(k)=P[X=k]$ in terms of $\widehat X(z)$ and $k$.

smt-2022-power-2-6.prompt: Let $X_n\sim\mathrm{Binomial}\left(n,\frac\lambda n\right)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$. Using that the $z$-transform determines the distribution (Problem 2.5), prove that $X_n$ converges in distribution to $Y$, i.e. that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat{X_n}(z)=\widehat Y(z)$ for every $z$. (Recall $\widehat{X_n}(z)=(1-p+pz)^n$ for $\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ and $\widehat Y(z)=e^{\lambda(z-1)}$.)

smt-2022-power-2-7.prompt: A *Poisson process* with parameter $\lambda$ is an arrival process in which the number of arrivals up to time $t$ is $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)$. The $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ distribution has density $p_X(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$. Prove that the inter-arrival time $X$ of a Poisson process with parameter $\lambda$ is distributed as $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. (Hint: compute the probability that there are no arrivals from time $0$ to time $t$.)

smt-2022-power-2-8a.prompt: Let $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, i.e. $X$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $x\ge0$. Compute $\mathbb E[X]$. Show your work.

smt-2022-power-2-8b.prompt: Let $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, i.e. $X$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $x\ge0$. Compute its moment generating function $\widetilde X(s)=\mathbb E[e^{sX}]$. Show your work.

smt-2022-power-2-8c.prompt: Let $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$ be independent (densities $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ and $\mu e^{-\mu y}$ on $[0,\infty)$). Compute $P[X<Y]$. Show your work.

smt-2022-power-3-1a.prompt: Consider an M/M/1/$\infty$ queue: customers arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, service times are independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$, there is one server, service is first-come first-served, and $\lambda<\mu$. In the steady state let $N$ be the number of people in the system (including the one being served) and $T$ the time an arriving customer spends in the system until leaving. Without using Little's Law, express $\mathbb E[N]$ and $\mathbb E[T]$ in terms of each other and $\mu$.

smt-2022-power-3-1b.prompt: Consider an M/M/1/$\infty$ queue: customers arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, service times are independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$, there is one server, service is first-come first-served, and $\lambda<\mu$. In the steady state let $N$ be the number of people in the system (including the one being served) and $T$ the time an arriving customer spends in the system until leaving. Without using Little's Law, compute $\mathbb E[N]$ and $\mathbb E[T]$ in terms of $\lambda$ and $\mu$. (It may help to use the traffic density $\rho=\lambda/\mu$.)

smt-2022-power-3-2a.prompt: Consider a queueing system with a steady state in which jobs arrive at average rate $\lambda$. Let $A(t)$ be the number of arrivals by time $t$, $C(t)$ the number of jobs that have been served (have left) by time $t$, $N(t')$ the number of jobs in the system at time $t'$, and $T_i$ the time job $i$ spends in the system (from arrival to departure). Assume $\lambda=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{A(t)}t=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{C(t)}t$. Define the time-average number of jobs in the system $\overline N$ and the time-average time in the system $\overline T$ in terms of these quantities.

smt-2022-power-3-2b.prompt: Consider a queueing system with a steady state in which jobs arrive at average rate $\lambda$. Let $A(t)$ be the number of arrivals by time $t$, $C(t)$ the number of jobs that have been served (have left) by time $t$, $N(t')$ the number of jobs in the system at time $t'$, and $T_i$ the time job $i$ spends in the system (from arrival to departure). Assume $\lambda=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{A(t)}t=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{C(t)}t$. Prove the time-average version of Little's Law: $\overline N=\lambda\overline T$, where $\overline N=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\int_0^tN(t')\,dt'$ and $\overline T=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i=1}^{A(t)}T_i=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1{C(t)}\sum_{i=1}^{C(t)}T_i$. (The system is empty at time $0$; you may use the squeeze theorem.)
smt-2022-power-3-2b.answer: $\overline N=\lambda\overline T$ (squeeze $\int_0^tN$ between $\sum_{i\le C(t)}T_i$ and $\sum_{i\le A(t)}T_i$).

smt-2022-power-3-3.prompt: Consider an M/M/1/$\infty$ queue: customers arrive according to a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, service times are independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$, there is one server, service is first-come first-served, and $\lambda<\mu$. In the steady state let $N$ be the number of people in the system (including the one being served) and $T$ the time an arriving customer spends in the system until leaving. Using Little's Law ($\mathbb E[N]=\lambda\mathbb E[T]$) and the relation $\mathbb E[T]=\frac{\mathbb E[N]+1}{\mu}$ (Problem 3.1(a)), rederive $\mathbb E[N]$ and $\mathbb E[T]$.

smt-2022-power-3-4.prompt: **PASTA.** Consider a queueing system whose arrivals form a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$ (exponential inter-arrival times). Let $a_n$ be the probability that an arriving customer sees $n$ people in the system, and let $\pi_n=\lim_{t\to\infty}P[N(t)=n]$ be the steady-state (time-average) probability of $n$ people in the system. Prove that $a_n=\pi_n$; precisely, $\lim_{t\to\infty}P[N(t)=n]=\lim_{t\to\infty}P[N(t)=n\mid\text{arrival happens right after time }t]$.
smt-2022-power-3-4.answer: $a_n=\pi_n$: the future arrival event is independent of $\{N(t)=n\}$ for Poisson arrivals.

smt-2022-power-3-5.prompt: Consider an M/M/$k$/0 queue: there are $k$ servers (stores) and no waiting room, customers arrive as a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$, each service takes an independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$ time, and an arriving customer who finds all $k$ servers busy is turned away. Let $\rho=\lambda/\mu$. Compute (with proof) the blocking probability $P_{\text{block}}$, the (time-average) probability that all $k$ servers are busy when a new customer arrives. (You may use PASTA, Problem 3.4, and the fact that the minimum of independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu_1)$, $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu_2)$ variables is $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu_1+\mu_2)$.)

smt-2022-power-4-1.prompt: A $(m,p)$ *kidney exchange market* consists of patient-donor pairs. Pairs arrive as a Poisson process of rate $m$; a newly arrived pair is linked to each pair already present independently with probability $p$ (write $d=pm$); and each pair in the market becomes *critical* at the points of an independent rate-$1$ Poisson process (so with $z$ pairs present, criticality events occur at total rate $z$). Linked pairs may be matched, and matched pairs leave the market; a pair that becomes critical leaves the market, matched or not. We say the market is in steady state when the arrival rate equals the departure rate. The *loss* of a matching algorithm is $L=C/m$, where $C$ is the time-average rate at which pairs become critical without having been matched. Suppose that no pairs are ever matched. If the system is in steady state, show that the expected number of pairs in the market that a newly arriving pair sees is $m$.

smt-2022-power-4-3a.prompt: Prove that for any nonnegative random variable $Y$ and any $k\ge0$, $\mathbb E[Y]\le k+\int_k^\infty P[Y>y]\,dy$.

smt-2022-power-4-3b.prompt: Let $f$ be an increasing function and $g$ a decreasing function of a real variable, and let $X$ be a random variable (for instance uniform on $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, or any nonnegative random variable, for which the expectations exist). Prove that $\mathbb E[f(X)g(X)]\le\mathbb E[f(X)]\,\mathbb E[g(X)]$.
smt-2022-power-4-3b.answer: Chebyshev's association inequality: use an independent copy $X'$ with $(f(X)-f(X'))(g(X)-g(X'))\le0$.

smt-2022-power-4-3c.prompt: A nonnegative integer-valued random variable $X$ is $(c_1,c_2,m)$ *well-concentrated* if $P\left[|X-\mathbb E[X]|>k\sqrt m\right]\le c_1\sqrt m\,e^{-c_2k^2}$ for all $k>0$. Suppose $X$ is $(c_1,c_2,m)$ well-concentrated with $c_1,c_2$ fixed, let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $d>1$ be fixed. Prove that for all sufficiently large $m$ $$\mathbb E\left[X\left(1-\frac dm\right)^X\right]\le\mathbb E[X]\,e^{-d\,\mathbb E[X]/m}(1+\varepsilon).$$ You may use $1+x\le e^x$, Problem 4.3(a) ($\mathbb E[Y]\le k+\int_k^\infty P[Y>y]dy$ for $Y\ge0$) and Problem 4.3(b) (for $f$ increasing and $g$ decreasing, $\mathbb E[f(X)g(X)]\le\mathbb E[f(X)]\mathbb E[g(X)]$).
smt-2022-power-4-3c.answer: By 4.3(b) the left side is $\le\mathbb E[X]\,\mathbb E[(1-d/m)^X]\le\mathbb E[X]\,\mathbb E[e^{-dX/m}]$, and concentration gives $\mathbb E[e^{-d(X-\mathbb E X)/m}]\le1+\varepsilon$ for large $m$.

smt-2022-power-4-4a.prompt: A $(m,p)$ *kidney exchange market* consists of patient-donor pairs. Pairs arrive as a Poisson process of rate $m$; a newly arrived pair is linked to each pair already present independently with probability $p$ (write $d=pm$); and each pair in the market becomes *critical* at the points of an independent rate-$1$ Poisson process (so with $z$ pairs present, criticality events occur at total rate $z$). Linked pairs may be matched, and matched pairs leave the market; a pair that becomes critical leaves the market, matched or not. We say the market is in steady state when the arrival rate equals the departure rate. The *loss* of a matching algorithm is $L=C/m$, where $C$ is the time-average rate at which pairs become critical without having been matched. The *patient algorithm* does nothing when a pair arrives; when a pair becomes critical and is linked to some pair present, it matches them (both leave); if the critical pair has no links it simply leaves. Suppose there are currently $z$ pairs in the market. If a pair becomes critical, what is the probability that it has a match?
smt-2022-power-4-4a.answer: $1-(1-p)^{z-1}$ (with $z$ pairs in total, including the critical one); asymptotically $\approx1-(1-p)^z$
smt-2022-power-4-4a.reviewNote: The official key gives 1-(1-p)^z, which is the probability when z counts the other pairs; with z the total market size the exact value is 1-(1-p)^(z-1). The difference is a factor 1-p -> 1 and does not affect Theorem 4.2.

smt-2022-power-5-1.prompt: Let $G=(V,E)$ be an undirected graph. Prove the Handshake Lemma: $\sum_{v\in V}\deg(v)=2|E|$.
smt-2022-power-5-1.answer: Each edge contributes $1$ to the degree of each of its two endpoints.

smt-2022-power-5-2.prompt: A graph $G=(V,E)$ has vertex set $V$ and a set $E$ of unordered pairs of distinct vertices (edges); $\deg(v)$ is the number of edges containing $v$. A *matching* is a set $M\subseteq E$ of edges with no common endpoints; it is *maximal* if no edge of $E\setminus M$ can be added to it keeping it a matching, and *maximum* if $|M|$ is largest possible. For each of the three graphs in the figure, the thick edges are highlighted. Say whether the highlighted edges form a maximal matching and whether they form a maximum matching. If they do not form a maximum matching, find a maximum matching. (No justification required.) Graph 1 has vertices $1,\dots,6$ with edges $3\text{-}6$, $3\text{-}5$, $2\text{-}6$, $2\text{-}5$, $2\text{-}4$, $1\text{-}6$, $1\text{-}5$, $1\text{-}4$ and highlighted $2\text{-}6$, $1\text{-}5$.
smt-2022-power-5-2.answer: Graph 1: maximal but not maximum; a maximum matching is $\{1\text{-}4,\,2\text{-}5,\,3\text{-}6\}$. Graph 2: maximal and maximum. Graph 3: neither; e.g. add $3\text{-}7$ (or $6\text{-}7$) to get a maximum matching of size 3.

smt-2022-power-5-3.prompt: A graph $G=(V,E)$ has vertex set $V$ and a set $E$ of unordered pairs of distinct vertices (edges); $\deg(v)$ is the number of edges containing $v$. A *matching* is a set $M\subseteq E$ of edges with no common endpoints; it is *maximal* if no edge of $E\setminus M$ can be added to it keeping it a matching, and *maximum* if $|M|$ is largest possible. Assume the following operations each take time $1$: checking whether a vertex is an endpoint of some edge in a list of edges, and adding an edge to a list. Propose an algorithm that computes a maximal matching of a graph $G=(V,E)$ with $m=|E|$ in time at most $c\cdot m$, prove the running time bound, and find $c$ for your algorithm.
smt-2022-power-5-3.answer: Scan the edges once, adding an edge if neither endpoint is already covered; $c=2$ (counting the two endpoint checks per edge), or at most $3$ if additions are counted too.

smt-2022-power-5-4.prompt: A graph $G=(V,E)$ has vertex set $V$ and a set $E$ of unordered pairs of distinct vertices (edges); $\deg(v)$ is the number of edges containing $v$. A *matching* is a set $M\subseteq E$ of edges with no common endpoints; it is *maximal* if no edge of $E\setminus M$ can be added to it keeping it a matching, and *maximum* if $|M|$ is largest possible. An *alternating path* with respect to a matching $M$ is a path $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_k$ whose consecutive edges alternate between being in $M$ and not in $M$. An *augmenting path* is an alternating path whose two endpoints $v_1,v_k$ are not covered by $M$. Prove Berge's Lemma: a matching $M$ is a maximum matching if and only if there is no augmenting path with respect to $M$.
smt-2022-power-5-4.answer: Augmenting path $\Rightarrow$ flip it to get a larger matching; non-maximum $M$ $\Rightarrow$ $M\triangle M'$ contains an augmenting path.

smt-2022-power-5-5a.prompt: Let $G=(X,Y,E)$ be a bipartite graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, and let $M$ be a matching. An augmenting path with respect to $M$ is a path whose edges alternate between non-$M$ and $M$ edges and whose two endpoints are not covered by $M$. Assume checking membership of a vertex or edge in a list and adding to a list each take time $1$. Propose an algorithm that either finds an augmenting path with respect to $M$ or reports that none exists, and prove that it is correct. (Hint: what does an augmenting path in a bipartite graph look like?)
smt-2022-power-5-5a.answer: Direct non-matching edges $X\to Y$ and matching edges $Y\to X$; BFS from all uncovered $x\in X$; an uncovered $y\in Y$ is reached iff an augmenting path exists.

An augmenting path with respect to $M$ is a path whose edges alternate between non-$M$ and $M$ edges and whose two endpoints are not covered by $M$. Assume checking membership of a vertex or edge in a list and adding to a list each take time $1$. For the alternating breadth-first search algorithm (direct non-matching edges $X\to Y$ and matching edges $Y\to X$, search from all uncovered vertices of $X$), prove that its running time is at most $c\,(n+m)$ for a constant $c$.
smt-2022-power-5-5b.answer: Each vertex is enqueued once and each directed edge scanned once: time $O(n+m)$.

smt-2022-power-5-5c.prompt: Let $G=(X,Y,E)$ be a bipartite graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, and let $M$ be a matching. An augmenting path with respect to $M$ is a path whose edges alternate between non-$M$ and $M$ edges and whose two endpoints are not covered by $M$. Assume checking membership of a vertex or edge in a list and adding to a list each take time $1$. Propose an algorithm for computing a maximum matching of a bipartite graph $G$ using the augmenting-path algorithm above, and give an upper bound on its running time (don't worry about constants).
smt-2022-power-5-5c.answer: Repeat: find an augmenting path and flip it; at most $n/2$ rounds; time $O(n(n+m))$.

smt-2022-power-5-6.prompt: A graph $G=(V,E)$ has vertex set $V$ and a set $E$ of unordered pairs of distinct vertices (edges); $\deg(v)$ is the number of edges containing $v$. A *matching* is a set $M\subseteq E$ of edges with no common endpoints; it is *maximal* if no edge of $E\setminus M$ can be added to it keeping it a matching, and *maximum* if $|M|$ is largest possible. Let $M$ be a maximal matching in a graph $G$ and $M'$ a maximum matching. Prove that $|M|\ge\frac12|M'|$.
smt-2022-power-5-6.answer: Every edge of $M'$ touches a vertex covered by $M$, so $|M'|\le|V(M)|=2|M|$.

smt-2022-power-6-1a.prompt: In *online bipartite matching*, $G=(X,Y,E)$ starts with all of $Y$ present and no vertices of $X$. The vertices of $X$ arrive one at a time together with their edges to $Y$; when $x$ arrives the algorithm must immediately either match it to a neighbour $y\in Y$ not yet matched, or leave it unmatched forever. The *performance* on input $(G,L)$ ($L$ the arrival order) is $\mathrm{ALG}(G,L)/|M^*|$ where $M^*$ is a maximum matching of $G$, and the *competitive ratio* is the minimum performance over all inputs. Propose a deterministic algorithm whose competitive ratio is at least $\frac12$.
smt-2022-power-6-1a.answer: Greedy: match each arriving $x$ to any free neighbour; it produces a maximal matching, which has size at least $\frac12|M^*|$.

smt-2022-power-6-1b.prompt: In *online bipartite matching*, $G=(X,Y,E)$ starts with all of $Y$ present and no vertices of $X$. The vertices of $X$ arrive one at a time together with their edges to $Y$; when $x$ arrives the algorithm must immediately either match it to a neighbour $y\in Y$ not yet matched, or leave it unmatched forever. The *performance* on input $(G,L)$ ($L$ the arrival order) is $\mathrm{ALG}(G,L)/|M^*|$ where $M^*$ is a maximum matching of $G$, and the *competitive ratio* is the minimum performance over all inputs. Prove that no deterministic online algorithm has competitive ratio greater than $\frac12$. (Hint: two vertices in $X$ suffice.)
smt-2022-power-6-1b.answer: Let $x_1\sim\{y_1,y_2\}$ arrive first; whatever it is matched to, let $x_2$ arrive adjacent only to that vertex.

smt-2022-power-6-2.prompt: A *fractional matching* of $G=(X,Y,E)$ assigns a number $m_{xy}\ge0$ to each edge such that $\sum_{y\in N(x)}m_{xy}\le1$ for each $x\in X$ and $\sum_{x\in N(y)}m_{xy}\le1$ for each $y\in Y$. A randomized online algorithm $\mathrm{ALG}$ chooses its matching decisions at random (based on the current graph and the arriving vertex). Prove that there is a deterministic online fractional algorithm $\mathrm{FracALG}$ producing a fractional matching $\{m_{xy}\}$ with $\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}(G,L)]=\sum_{(x,y)\in E}m_{xy}$ at the end, and briefly describe why one can also go from a deterministic fractional algorithm to a randomized one.

smt-2022-power-6-3.prompt: In a fractional online algorithm each arriving $x$ brings one unit of money which is distributed as it increases $m_{xy}$: let $a_x$ and $b_y$ be the (nonnegative) money collected by $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$, arranged so that $\sum_{(x,y)\in E}m_{xy}=\sum_xa_x+\sum_yb_y$. Prove that if the money satisfies $a_x+b_y\ge c$ for every edge $(x,y)\in E$ at the end, then the fractional algorithm is $c$-competitive, i.e. $\sum m_{xy}\ge c\,|M^*|$ where $M^*$ is a maximum matching. (Hint: compare with the optimal matching.)

smt-2022-power-6-4a.prompt: The *Water Level algorithm* is a fractional online algorithm: when $x$ arrives with neighbourhood $N(x)$ and has a budget of $1$, it repeatedly increases $m_{xy}$ for the neighbour(s) $y\in N(x)$ whose load $W_y=\sum_{x'}m_{x'y}$ is currently smallest (raising the lowest loads equally), until the budget is used up or all neighbours have load $1$. Loads never exceed $1$. For a fixed increasing differentiable $g:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with antiderivative $G$, money is assigned as follows: when $m_{xy}$ is increased by $dm$ at the moment $y$ has load $W_y$, $y$ receives $g(W_y)\,dm$ and $x$ receives $(1-g(W_y))\,dm$. Hence $b_y=\int_0^{W_y}g(s)\,ds$. Fix an edge $(x,y)\in E$ and let $W_y^f$ be the final load of $y$. Prove that if $W_y^f=1$ then $a_x+b_y\ge G(1)-G(0)$.

smt-2022-power-6-4b.prompt: The *Water Level algorithm* is a fractional online algorithm: when $x$ arrives with neighbourhood $N(x)$ and has a budget of $1$, it repeatedly increases $m_{xy}$ for the neighbour(s) $y\in N(x)$ whose load $W_y=\sum_{x'}m_{x'y}$ is currently smallest (raising the lowest loads equally), until the budget is used up or all neighbours have load $1$. Loads never exceed $1$. For a fixed increasing differentiable $g:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with antiderivative $G$, money is assigned as follows: when $m_{xy}$ is increased by $dm$ at the moment $y$ has load $W_y$, $y$ receives $g(W_y)\,dm$ and $x$ receives $(1-g(W_y))\,dm$. Hence $b_y=\int_0^{W_y}g(s)\,ds$. Fix an edge $(x,y)\in E$ and let $W_y^f$ be the final load of $y$. Prove that $a_x+b_y\ge G(W_y^f)-G(0)+1-g(W_y^f)$.
smt-2022-power-6-4b.answer: $b_y=G(W_y^f)-G(0)$, and $x$ collected at least $1-g(W_y^f)$ per unit of its budget.
smt-2022-power-6-4b.reviewNote: As printed the inequality a_x+b_y >= G(W)-G(0)+1-g(W) is only justified for W_y^f < 1 (x may collect little money if all neighbours are full); for W_y^f = 1 the weaker bound of 6.4(a) is the one that holds and suffices.

smt-2022-power-6-4c.prompt: The *Water Level algorithm* is a fractional online algorithm: when $x$ arrives with neighbourhood $N(x)$ and has a budget of $1$, it repeatedly increases $m_{xy}$ for the neighbour(s) $y\in N(x)$ whose load $W_y=\sum_{x'}m_{x'y}$ is currently smallest (raising the lowest loads equally), until the budget is used up or all neighbours have load $1$. Loads never exceed $1$. For a fixed increasing differentiable $g:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with antiderivative $G$, money is assigned as follows: when $m_{xy}$ is increased by $dm$ at the moment $y$ has load $W_y$, $y$ receives $g(W_y)\,dm$ and $x$ receives $(1-g(W_y))\,dm$. Hence $b_y=\int_0^{W_y}g(s)\,ds$. We want a function $g$ with $G(1)-G(0)=c$ and $G(z)-G(0)+1-g(z)=c$ for all $z\in[0,1]$ (then every edge has $a_x+b_y\ge c$ by 6.4(a),(b)). Find such a $g$ and compute the resulting competitive ratio $c$.

smt-2022-power-6-5a.prompt: Let $G_n=(X,Y,E)$ with $X=Y=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and edges $E=\{(x,y):y\ge x\}$. Show that the maximum matching of $G_n$ has size $n$.
smt-2022-power-6-5a.answer: The edges $(i,i)$ form a perfect matching.

smt-2022-power-6-5b.prompt: Let $G_n=(X,Y,E)$ with $X=Y=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and edges $E=\{(x,y):y\ge x\}$. The vertices of $X$ arrive in the order $1,2,\dots,n$ and the Water Level algorithm is run (each arriving $x$ distributes budget $1$ among its neighbours $\{x,x+1,\dots,n\}$, always raising the lowest loads). Prove that as $n\to\infty$ the competitive ratio of Water Level on this input tends to $1-\frac1e$. (You may use $H_n=\ln n+\gamma+o(1)$.)
smt-2022-power-6-5b.answer: After $i$ arrivals the loads of $y\ge i$ equal $\sum_{t\le i}\frac1{n-t+1}$; they reach $1$ when $i\approx n(1-\frac1e)$, so Water Level matches $\approx n(1-\frac1e)$.

smt-2022-power-6-5c.prompt: Let $G_n=(X,Y,E)$ with $X=Y=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and edges $E=\{(x,y):y\ge x\}$. Let $\mathrm{ALG}$ be a randomized integral online matching algorithm run on $G_n$, where the vertices $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $X$ arrive in this order and the labels of $Y$ are permuted by a uniformly random permutation (so $x_i$ is adjacent to a set $S_i$ of $n-i+1$ vertices of $Y$ with $S_1\supset S_2\supset\cdots$, where $S_{i+1}$ is $S_i$ minus a uniformly random element). Prove that the expected size of the matching satisfies $$\frac1n\,\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}]\le\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\min\left(1,\sum_{i=1}^j\frac1{n-i+1}\right).$$ (Hint: first deterministic algorithms.)
smt-2022-power-6-5c.answer: For the vertex $y^{(j)}$ removed after step $j$: $P[\text{matched to }x_i]\le\frac1{n-i+1}$ for $i\le j$; sum and cap by $1$.
smt-2022-power-6-5c.reviewNote: The printed statement says 'we choose a random ordering L of {1,...,n}'. With a fixed graph G_n and a uniformly random arrival order of X the bound is false (matching each arriving x to its smallest-labelled free neighbour always finds a perfect matching). The bound holds, and is proved here, for the standard hard instance: X arrives in order 1..n and the labels of Y are randomly permuted.

smt-2022-power-6-5d.prompt: Let $G_n=(X,Y,E)$ with $X=Y=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and edges $E=\{(x,y):y\ge x\}$. Suppose the right-hand side $\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\min\left(1,\sum_{i\le j}\frac1{n-i+1}\right)$ of Problem 6.5(c) tends to $1-\frac1e$ as $n\to\infty$. Show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is some $n$ and an input (a labelling/arrival order) $L_n$ on which any randomized integral algorithm has $\frac1n\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}(G_n,L_n)]\le1-\frac1e+\varepsilon$; consequently no randomized algorithm has competitive ratio better than $1-\frac1e$.
smt-2022-power-6-5d.answer: An average over orderings is at most the bound, so some fixed ordering is at most the bound.

smt-2022-power-7-1a.prompt: In a *stable matching problem* there are $n$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$; every student $h$ has a strict preference ranking $L_h$ of all schools and every school $s$ a strict ranking $L_s$ of all students ($a\succ b$ means $a$ is preferred to $b$). A perfect matching $M$ pairs every student with a distinct school. A pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$ is *unstable* if $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$; $M$ is *stable* if it has no unstable pair. The *proposal algorithm*: start with $M=\emptyset$; while some student $h$ is unmatched, $h$ proposes to the highest-ranked school on $L_h$ that has not yet received a proposal from $h$; if that school $s$ is unmatched, add $(h,s)$ to $M$; if $s$ is matched to $h'$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$, replace $(h',s)$ by $(h,s)$ (and $h'$ becomes unmatched); otherwise $h$ is rejected. Return $M$. Prove that the proposal algorithm terminates, and give an upper bound on the number of iterations of the loop.
smt-2022-power-7-1a.answer: Each student proposes to each school at most once, so at most $n^2$ iterations.

smt-2022-power-7-1b.prompt: In a *stable matching problem* there are $n$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$; every student $h$ has a strict preference ranking $L_h$ of all schools and every school $s$ a strict ranking $L_s$ of all students ($a\succ b$ means $a$ is preferred to $b$). A perfect matching $M$ pairs every student with a distinct school. A pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$ is *unstable* if $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$; $M$ is *stable* if it has no unstable pair. The *proposal algorithm*: start with $M=\emptyset$; while some student $h$ is unmatched, $h$ proposes to the highest-ranked school on $L_h$ that has not yet received a proposal from $h$; if that school $s$ is unmatched, add $(h,s)$ to $M$; if $s$ is matched to $h'$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$, replace $(h',s)$ by $(h,s)$ (and $h'$ becomes unmatched); otherwise $h$ is rejected. Return $M$. Prove that the matching $M$ returned by the proposal algorithm is full: $|M|=n$.
smt-2022-power-7-1b.answer: An unmatched student would have proposed to every school, so every school would be matched, contradicting an unmatched student when $|S|=|H|$.

smt-2022-power-7-2.prompt: In a *stable matching problem* there are $n$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$; every student $h$ has a strict preference ranking $L_h$ of all schools and every school $s$ a strict ranking $L_s$ of all students ($a\succ b$ means $a$ is preferred to $b$). A perfect matching $M$ pairs every student with a distinct school. A pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$ is *unstable* if $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$; $M$ is *stable* if it has no unstable pair. The *proposal algorithm*: start with $M=\emptyset$; while some student $h$ is unmatched, $h$ proposes to the highest-ranked school on $L_h$ that has not yet received a proposal from $h$; if that school $s$ is unmatched, add $(h,s)$ to $M$; if $s$ is matched to $h'$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$, replace $(h',s)$ by $(h,s)$ (and $h'$ becomes unmatched); otherwise $h$ is rejected. Return $M$. Prove that the proposal algorithm returns a stable matching.
smt-2022-power-7-2.answer: Students only move down their lists, schools only move up theirs; an unstable pair would contradict this.

smt-2022-power-7-3.prompt: In a *stable matching problem* there are $n$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$; every student $h$ has a strict preference ranking $L_h$ of all schools and every school $s$ a strict ranking $L_s$ of all students ($a\succ b$ means $a$ is preferred to $b$). A perfect matching $M$ pairs every student with a distinct school. A pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$ is *unstable* if $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$; $M$ is *stable* if it has no unstable pair. The *proposal algorithm*: start with $M=\emptyset$; while some student $h$ is unmatched, $h$ proposes to the highest-ranked school on $L_h$ that has not yet received a proposal from $h$; if that school $s$ is unmatched, add $(h,s)$ to $M$; if $s$ is matched to $h'$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$, replace $(h',s)$ by $(h,s)$ (and $h'$ becomes unmatched); otherwise $h$ is rejected. Return $M$. For a student $h$ let $\mathrm{best}(h)$ be the highest-ranked school he is matched to in any stable matching, and for a school $s$ let $\mathrm{worst}(s)$ be the lowest-ranked student it is matched to in any stable matching. Prove that the matching returned by the proposal algorithm is both *student-optimal* ($M=\{(h,\mathrm{best}(h))\}$) and *school-pessimal* ($M=\{(\mathrm{worst}(s),s)\}$).
smt-2022-power-7-3.answer: No student is ever rejected by his best stable partner (first-rejection argument); then each school ends with its worst stable partner.

smt-2022-power-7-4.prompt: In a *stable matching problem* there are $n$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$; every student $h$ has a strict preference ranking $L_h$ of all schools and every school $s$ a strict ranking $L_s$ of all students ($a\succ b$ means $a$ is preferred to $b$). A perfect matching $M$ pairs every student with a distinct school. A pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$ is *unstable* if $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$; $M$ is *stable* if it has no unstable pair. The *proposal algorithm*: start with $M=\emptyset$; while some student $h$ is unmatched, $h$ proposes to the highest-ranked school on $L_h$ that has not yet received a proposal from $h$; if that school $s$ is unmatched, add $(h,s)$ to $M$; if $s$ is matched to $h'$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$, replace $(h',s)$ by $(h,s)$ (and $h'$ becomes unmatched); otherwise $h$ is rejected. Return $M$. A pair $(h,s)$ are *soulmates* if they are matched in every stable matching. Give an algorithm which, given a stable matching problem, determines whether there is a pair of soulmates (and returns one if so).
smt-2022-power-7-4.answer: Run the proposal algorithm with students proposing and with schools proposing; any pair common to both outputs is a pair of soulmates, and there is none if the outputs share no pair.

smt-2022-power-7-5.prompt: Suppose there are $mn$ students $H$ and $n$ schools $S$, where each school $s$ has $m$ spots. Every student has a strict ranking $L_h$ of the schools and every school a strict ranking $L_s$ of the students. A matching assigns each student to a school with each school receiving exactly $m$ students. A pair $(h,s)$ with $h$ assigned to $s'\ne s$ is *unstable* if $s\succ s'$ in $L_h$ and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$ for some student $h'$ assigned to $s$. Prove that a stable matching (one with no unstable pair) exists. (Hint: how can you simulate $mn$ schools?) You may use the existence of stable matchings in the one-to-one setting (Theorem 7.1).
smt-2022-power-7-5.answer: Replace each school by $m$ copies with identical preference lists and reduce to the one-to-one case.
